title: Indexes Follow Queries
hook: The right index for one query can be wasted work for every write.
premise: Use a relational workload with known filters, ordering, and row counts. Index selection is a measured read/write trade-off, not a checklist of popular columns.
roadmap: Name the query
Record predicates, sort order, returned fields, and representative parameter distributions.
Inspect the plan
Compare estimated and actual row counts in an authorized test environment.
Choose column order
Match the index to useful leading predicates and ordering, considering the engine's access methods.
Measure write cost
Track insert, update, storage, and maintenance effects alongside read latency.
Test skew and growth
Use realistic selectivity and data volume rather than only a tiny uniform fixture.
Retire unused indexes
Review sustained usage and dependencies before removing redundant index maintenance.
decisions: Composite index
Choose a composite index for a demonstrated multi-column filter or ordering pattern.
Column order and selectivity matter; one index is not automatically useful for every predicate combination.
Covering access
Include needed fields when index-only access can reduce costly table fetches.
Larger indexes cost storage and writes, and visibility rules may still require table access.
Sequential scan
Accept a scan when the query reads much of a small or broad dataset.
Forcing an index can make a broad query slower; compare actual work rather than visual plan labels.
incident: Notice query regression
A once-fast query slows after data growth or a changed parameter distribution.
Compare row estimates
Check whether statistics and selectivity assumptions match the current data.
Inspect lock and I/O waits
Distinguish a poor access path from waiting caused by another transaction or storage pressure.
Test one index candidate
Evaluate the candidate with representative read and write traffic.
Deploy with a safe method
Choose the engine-supported index-build procedure and understand its lock behavior.
Measure the new balance
Confirm lower query cost without unacceptable write latency or storage growth.
metrics: Rows scanned
Measure examined rows relative to returned rows for the target query class.
High scan counts are not automatically bad for intentionally broad analytical queries.
Write latency
Track mutation latency before and after adding the index.
An index that helps one dashboard may slow every write in a hot table.
Estimate error
Compare planner row estimates with observed rows under representative parameters.
Stale or insufficient statistics can mislead the planner even when a useful index exists.
lab: Create skewed data
Seed a local table with both common and rare filter values.
Record query plans
Capture plans for selective lookups and broad range scans.
Add a composite index
Match it to one concrete predicate and ordering pattern.
Repeat the workload
Keep the dataset and cache conditions explicit between measurements.
Measure mutations
Run inserts and updates to expose maintenance costs.
Explain the trade-off
Document which queries improved, which did not, and why.
takeaway: An index is a workload-specific data structure with a write bill attached.

title: Database Pools Need a Budget
hook: Adding ten API replicas can accidentally multiply database connections by ten.
premise: Treat the database connection limit as a shared budget across application replicas, workers, migrations, and administrative recovery paths.
roadmap: Count all clients
Include API nodes, background workers, dashboards, and maintenance jobs in the connection inventory.
Reserve headroom
Keep capacity for administration and failover rather than allocating every slot to normal traffic.
Bound acquisition waits
Set a finite wait for a connection and expose queue time separately from query time.
Shorten transactions
Avoid holding connections during unrelated network calls or user interaction.
Use pooling deliberately
Check session-state assumptions before enabling transaction-level proxy pooling.
Test deployment peaks
Account for old and new replicas coexisting during rolling updates and autoscaling.
decisions: Application pool
Use an application pool to reuse connections and cap each process's demand.
Per-process limits do not create a global budget when the replica count changes.
Transaction pooler
Use a compatible pooler when many clients can share fewer backend sessions.
Session variables, prepared statements, and transaction behavior need compatibility review.
Admission control
Limit active database work before it enters a saturated pool.
Rejecting or queueing work requires a clear deadline and client-visible overload behavior.
incident: Observe connection exhaustion
New requests fail to acquire sessions after a deployment or scale-out event.
Count actual sessions
Group sessions by application, state, transaction age, and ownership.
Protect recovery access
Preserve administrative capacity and reduce new application demand.
Find idle transactions
Inspect transactions that hold resources while doing no useful database work.
Rebalance pool sizes
Allocate the shared budget across the real maximum replica count.
Exercise the next rollout
Test overlapping replicas and worker restarts before repeating the deployment.
metrics: Pool wait time
Measure time spent waiting for an available connection.
Increasing pool size can move the queue into the database instead of removing it.
Transaction age
Track long-lived and idle-in-transaction sessions separately.
A quiet session can still retain locks or prevent cleanup progress.
Aggregate connections
Count all backend sessions against the reserved global budget.
The limit must cover deployment overlap, not only steady-state replica counts.
lab: Set a small budget
Use a disposable database with a deliberately limited session count.
Run several clients
Start API and worker processes with explicit pool limits.
Add rollout overlap
Launch replacement processes before stopping the old ones.
Hold one transaction
Simulate a slow external call while a connection remains checked out.
Bound the waits
Add admission and acquisition deadlines, then compare failure behavior.
Verify recovery headroom
Confirm an administrative session remains available during overload.
takeaway: A pool is a concurrency control, not permission to consume every database connection.

title: Read Replicas and Stale Truth
hook: A successful write followed by a missing read may be a routing decision, not lost data.
premise: Assume asynchronous replication. Replicas can improve read capacity, but freshness and read-your-writes behavior require an explicit application contract.
roadmap: Classify read freshness
Separate stale-tolerant browsing from security, billing, and immediate post-write confirmation.
Measure replay delay
Track replication progress and lag using the database's documented signals.
Route sensitive reads
Use an authoritative path when stale data could violate a correctness or authorization requirement.
Define session consistency
Choose primary reads, a consistency token, or another tested policy for read-your-writes flows.
Handle lagged replicas
Remove or limit replicas that exceed the accepted freshness budget.
Test promotion carefully
Verify failover, routing, and data-loss assumptions rather than treating a replica as a backup.
decisions: Primary reads
Use the primary for operations that require the latest committed state under the chosen database contract.
The primary remains a capacity dependency; optimize access rather than routing blindly.
Stale-tolerant replica
Use a replica for reads whose product contract permits delayed updates.
Users need defined behavior during lag and after recent writes.
Consistency-aware routing
Use a token or session policy when only selected reads require a freshness boundary.
Token propagation and replica eligibility add complexity that must survive failures.
incident: Observe missing recent writes
A client writes successfully but immediately reads old state.
Check the destination
Identify whether the read reached the primary or a lagging replica.
Inspect replication progress
Compare replay state with the write's committed position where supported.
Route conservatively
Send correctness-sensitive reads to an authoritative healthy path.
Recover replication
Fix the underlying replay, network, or capacity problem without hiding stale data.
Test the user journey
Repeat write-then-read behavior during normal operation, lag, and failover.
metrics: Replay lag
Track replication delay and replay progress with engine-specific semantics.
A time estimate alone may be misleading when no new writes are being generated.
Freshness misses
Measure observed stale reads in controlled journeys that require recent state.
Replica availability does not establish that it is fresh enough for every endpoint.
Primary fallback load
Track additional primary traffic when replicas become ineligible.
A lag event can create a fallback surge that overloads the authoritative node.
lab: Define two read classes
Create browsing and immediate-confirmation endpoints with different freshness needs.
Introduce replica delay
Use an authorized local replication test or a delayed read-model simulator.
Run write-then-read
Record routing and returned versions for the same logical object.
Apply a freshness policy
Route confirmation reads using a documented primary or token-based rule.
Fail a replica
Verify fallback remains bounded and does not expose stale authorization state.
Document the guarantee
State exactly which reads may lag and how the client observes that condition.
takeaway: Read capacity and read consistency are separate design decisions.

title: Transactions Protect Invariants
hook: Two individually valid requests can still create one invalid shared state.
premise: Use a last-item reservation example. Decide which database constraint or transaction pattern enforces the invariant under concurrent updates.
roadmap: Write the invariant
State the condition that must never be violated, such as one active owner per resource.
Place the boundary
Enforce uniqueness or conditional state changes at the database, not only in application prechecks.
Choose isolation deliberately
Understand which anomalies the chosen isolation level permits for this access pattern.
Keep transactions short
Avoid external calls and unnecessary scans while locks or snapshots are retained.
Handle conflicts explicitly
Retry only safe transactions with bounded attempts and a stable operation identity.
Test interleavings
Use two controlled sessions to reproduce the race and prove the intended outcome.
decisions: Unique constraint
Use a constraint when the invariant can be expressed as uniqueness or a relational check.
Application code still needs to interpret violations as expected conflicts rather than generic failures.
Conditional update
Use a state transition that succeeds only when the current value matches the expected condition.
Check the affected-row result and define behavior when another writer wins.
Serializable transaction
Use stronger isolation when the invariant spans reads and writes that need serializable reasoning.
Serialization failures are expected control flow and require safe bounded retry handling.
incident: Find the broken invariant
Two clients appear to own the same exclusive resource.
Reconstruct the race
Record the read and write sequence from each transaction.
Stop unsafe new claims
Protect the invariant while preserving evidence and existing valid ownership.
Move enforcement inward
Add the appropriate database constraint or atomic transition.
Reconcile existing state
Repair invalid records with a reviewed business rule, not an arbitrary winner.
Make the race deterministic
Add a two-session regression test that forces the original interleaving.
metrics: Conflict outcomes
Count expected constraint or serialization conflicts separately from unexpected database errors.
Some conflicts show protection working; hiding them can obscure contention and client behavior.
Lock wait time
Measure waits and transaction duration for the protected resource.
A correct invariant can still have poor throughput if transactions hold locks unnecessarily.
Invariant violations
Audit the business condition against authoritative stored state.
Successful HTTP responses are not evidence that a cross-row invariant always held.
lab: Model the final item
Create one reservable resource and two synthetic clients.
Force the naive race
Make both clients read availability before either writes.
Enforce ownership
Add a unique constraint or conditional update that can have only one winner.
Retry the winner
Reuse the operation identity and verify the original result is returned.
Inject a conflict
Test the client's response to a serialization or uniqueness conflict.
Audit final state
Assert the invariant after every tested interleaving and error path.
takeaway: The transaction is useful only when its boundary matches the business invariant.

title: The Transactional Outbox
hook: Updating a row and publishing an event are not one atomic operation by default.
premise: A service owns relational state and must notify other systems. The outbox closes one dual-write gap, but downstream delivery can still repeat.
roadmap: Define the event contract
Choose a stable event ID, schema version, and business meaning.
Commit state and event
Write the business change and outbox record in the same database transaction.
Relay durably
Publish pending outbox records through a worker or supported change-data-capture path.
Expect duplicate delivery
A relay can crash after publishing but before recording success.
Deduplicate downstream effects
Make consumers safe for repeated event IDs and define per-entity ordering requirements.
Manage retention and repair
Monitor old records, preserve replay evidence, and remove entries according to a documented policy.
decisions: Polling relay
Use polling for a straightforward outbox with predictable volume and acceptable delay.
Polling adds database work and needs careful claims, batching, and retry behavior.
Change-data capture
Use a supported CDC pipeline when change-log integration fits the operational environment.
Connector offsets, schema evolution, retention, and recovery become critical dependencies.
Direct dual write
Use separate writes only when missing notifications are acceptable or independently reconciled.
A crash between the writes can leave state and events inconsistent.
incident: Notice missing downstream state
The source database changed but a dependent projection never received the event.
Check the outbox record
Determine whether state and event were committed together.
Inspect relay progress
Compare oldest pending records with relay errors and broker acknowledgements.
Replay by identity
Republish the durable event using its original stable identity.
Verify consumer deduplication
Ensure repair does not repeat an irreversible side effect.
Test both crash windows
Fail before commit and after publish to validate the full handoff.
metrics: Oldest outbox age
Measure delay from business commit to successful relay progress.
A growing age can expose a stuck publisher even when total row count is small.
Relay attempts
Track publish attempts per event and permanent error categories.
Repeated delivery is expected at some boundaries; repeated business effects are not.
Projection freshness
Measure how far dependent read models lag behind committed source events.
A healthy broker does not prove every consumer has applied the latest state.
lab: Create one transaction
Write an order change and outbox row atomically in a local database.
Crash before commit
Verify that neither the order change nor its event becomes visible.
Crash after publish
Stop the relay before it marks the outbox row as delivered.
Restart the relay
Observe duplicate delivery with the same event identity.
Deduplicate the consumer
Apply the event through a durable consumer identity check.
Verify the final state
Assert one business effect and eventual projection convergence after recovery.
takeaway: An outbox makes the database handoff atomic, not the entire distributed workflow exactly once.

title: Choose the Shard Key Last
hook: A shard key can distribute bytes evenly while concentrating every important request on one shard.
premise: Consider partitioning only after measuring storage, throughput, contention, and query constraints. Distribution must fit access patterns, not just row counts.
roadmap: Map access patterns
List point lookups, ranges, joins, writes, and tenant-local operations.
Measure skew
Identify hot entities, time ranges, and workload imbalance before selecting a partition key.
Choose a routing contract
Define how clients locate data and how routing changes during movement.
Plan cross-shard work
Account for fan-out queries, distributed transactions, and global uniqueness needs.
Design rebalancing
Move data with explicit ownership, consistency checks, and rollback or forward-repair rules.
Test hotspots and growth
Exercise skewed traffic and a growing partition, not only uniform random keys.
decisions: Hash partitioning
Use hashing when even key distribution and point access dominate.
Range queries and locality-sensitive operations may require expensive fan-out.
Range partitioning
Use ranges when ordered scans and data lifecycle operations matter.
Monotonic keys and popular ranges can create write hotspots.
Tenant partitioning
Use tenant boundaries when most operations and isolation needs are tenant-local.
Very large tenants may outgrow a shard and require a separate migration strategy.
incident: Find one overloaded shard
A subset of keys has high latency while most shards remain lightly used.
Separate size from traffic
Compare bytes, active requests, and expensive operations by partition.
Contain the hot workload
Apply targeted admission or caching without assuming all shards need more capacity.
Review the key choice
Determine whether access locality or a monotonic key caused concentration.
Move data safely
Use a tested ownership-transfer protocol with reconciliation.
Verify skewed load
Replay the real key distribution and check cross-shard query costs.
metrics: Shard utilization spread
Compare resource demand across shards rather than only cluster averages.
Uniform row counts do not imply uniform CPU, I/O, or request cost.
Fan-out width
Measure how many partitions each query touches.
Adding shards can make a global query slower even while individual shards become smaller.
Rebalance backlog
Track data movement, validation progress, and ownership transitions.
A migration that copies bytes but loses updates is not a successful rebalance.
lab: Create a skewed keyset
Generate tenants with very different sizes and request popularity.
Simulate routing
Compare hash, range, and tenant-based assignments.
Run representative queries
Include point reads, ranges, and one global aggregation.
Inject a hot key
Concentrate demand and observe whether extra shards help.
Move one partition
Model ownership transfer while concurrent updates continue.
Check invariants
Verify no lost writes, duplicate ownership, or unexplained routing gaps.
takeaway: Shard for measured access patterns, and budget for movement and cross-shard work.

title: A Backup Is Not a Restore
hook: The first time you restore a backup should not be during the incident.
premise: Define recovery-point and recovery-time objectives for a disposable database example. Include logs, encryption keys, versions, and dependent configuration.
roadmap: Define acceptable loss
State the recovery-point objective and which business records must survive.
Define acceptable downtime
Set a recovery-time objective based on a complete usable service, not just copied files.
Capture required dependencies
Include logs, metadata, key access, compatible versions, and restoration permissions.
Protect backup isolation
Keep recovery copies protected from the same mistakes or compromised credentials as primary data.
Run a restore drill
Restore into an isolated environment and validate business invariants.
Measure the real recovery
Record download, replay, verification, routing, and application readiness time.
decisions: Logical backup
Use a logical export when portability and selective restoration fit the dataset and engine.
Large restores may be slow, and engine-specific objects or permissions need separate treatment.
Physical backup plus logs
Use physical recovery when engine-supported point-in-time restoration fits the recovery objective.
Version compatibility, log continuity, and configuration become part of the recovery contract.
Replica for availability
Use replication to reduce failover time for some infrastructure failures.
Replication can copy accidental deletion or corruption; it is not a substitute for isolated recovery copies.
incident: Freeze destructive changes
Preserve evidence and prevent automated jobs from worsening the data loss.
Choose a recovery point
Identify a safe point before the damaging event and quantify expected data loss.
Restore in isolation
Avoid overwriting the only remaining evidence or source of valid records.
Validate business data
Check identities, counts, references, and critical invariants before reopening traffic.
Reconcile later writes
Use a reviewed plan for legitimate updates after the chosen recovery point.
Document actual recovery time
Measure the whole workflow and update the runbook with observed bottlenecks.
metrics: Restore success
Track completed restoration drills with data validation, not only successful backup commands.
A green backup job can coexist with missing keys or an unusable restoration procedure.
Recovery duration
Measure time until the application is usable and verified.
File transfer time excludes replay, validation, configuration, and traffic restoration.
Recoverable window
Track log continuity and the latest point that can actually be restored.
Retention settings and missing log segments can silently narrow the promised recovery window.
lab: Seed identifiable records
Create synthetic records with known counts and referential relationships.
Take a recovery copy
Capture the database and the dependencies required by your chosen method.
Make a destructive change
Delete a known subset in the disposable environment.
Restore separately
Recover into a fresh instance using the documented procedure.
Verify exact outcomes
Check which records and updates should exist at the selected recovery point.
Time the full drill
Include application connection and validation before declaring recovery complete.
takeaway: Recovery is a tested workflow with measured loss and time, not a file that exists somewhere.

title: Schema Changes Without Surprises
hook: A migration can succeed while the old application version is still serving traffic.
premise: Assume rolling deployments where old and new application versions overlap. Schema compatibility must cover that overlap and the rollback window.
roadmap: Map version compatibility
List which application versions can read and write each schema state.
Expand first
Add compatible structures before requiring new readers or writers to use them.
Backfill incrementally
Use bounded batches with progress markers and a plan for concurrent updates.
Validate both paths
Compare old and new representations before switching authoritative reads.
Switch deliberately
Move traffic with observability and a clear rollback or forward-fix decision.
Contract later
Remove old fields only after old clients and the rollback window are retired.
decisions: Additive change
Prefer an additive change when old and new versions must coexist.
Temporary duplicate fields or paths need reconciliation and a clear retirement owner.
Blocking migration
Use a blocking change only when the maintenance window and lock impact are acceptable.
A small development table does not predict lock duration on production-sized data.
Online backfill
Use incremental backfill for large datasets with active writes.
Checkpointing and update races must be tested so a completed counter does not hide stale values.
incident: Identify incompatible traffic
Errors appear only on old application instances after the migration.
Check the compatibility matrix
Find which query or write contract no longer matches the database.
Stop further contraction
Pause destructive cleanup and preserve the old representation where possible.
Choose rollback or repair
Use the preplanned data-compatible recovery path instead of blindly reverting application code.
Validate backfilled rows
Compare sampled and invariant-based checks across the full dataset.
Add mixed-version tests
Run old and new clients against each transitional schema state.
metrics: Backfill progress
Track processed ranges, retries, and remaining rows with durable checkpoints.
A percentage alone does not show whether concurrent writes were incorporated correctly.
Lock duration
Measure blocking and transaction impact during each schema operation.
An operation called online may still take locks at important phases.
Representation drift
Compare old and new values while both paths exist.
Matching row counts do not prove equivalent business meaning or complete transformation.
lab: Create two clients
Run old and new application versions against a disposable database.
Add the new field
Introduce a nullable or otherwise compatible representation.
Backfill under writes
Update existing rows while synthetic clients continue changing data.
Compare semantics
Check that both representations describe the same business state.
Test rollback timing
Revert application traffic before and after the switch point.
Retire the old path
Remove it only after demonstrating that no supported client still depends on it.
takeaway: Expand, migrate, verify, then contract; deployment overlap is part of the schema contract.

title: Object Storage Has a Lifecycle
hook: The database row was deleted, but the expensive file was not.
premise: Use an application that stores file metadata in a database and bytes in object storage. Define ownership, publication, deletion, and retention across both systems.
roadmap: Define object ownership
Bind each object key to a verified tenant and business record.
Separate upload from publication
Keep incomplete or unvalidated uploads outside the public serving path.
Record authoritative metadata
Store version, size, and state needed to reconcile the object with the application.
Make deletion recoverable
Use a durable deletion request and replay-safe cleanup rather than a fragile dual write.
Apply retention rules
Distinguish business retention, legal requirements, versioning, and temporary upload cleanup.
Audit the inventory
Compare referenced and unreferenced objects without exposing private filenames or data.
decisions: Immediate deletion
Use immediate deletion when policy permits it and the operation can be retried safely.
A lost cleanup request can leave orphaned bytes unless a durable reconciliation path exists.
Soft deletion
Use a recoverable state when accidental deletion and support recovery matter.
Retention costs and authorization behavior must remain explicit while the data still exists.
Lifecycle policy
Use storage lifecycle rules for well-defined age or state transitions.
Age-based rules do not understand every application reference or business exception.
incident: Notice storage drift
Object-storage cost grows faster than the application's active data footprint.
Compare authoritative inventories
Identify unreferenced objects and incomplete multipart uploads.
Protect valid content
Exclude live and retained business records before any cleanup.
Repair the deletion workflow
Persist cleanup requests and make repeated deletion safe.
Recover interrupted jobs
Replay outstanding cleanup with bounded rate and audit records.
Verify the new lifecycle
Test upload failure, publication failure, deletion retries, and retention exceptions.
metrics: Unreferenced bytes
Estimate storage not associated with a valid current or retained business record.
Unreferenced does not automatically mean deletable; retention and recovery policies still apply.
Cleanup age
Track the oldest pending deletion or abandoned-upload task.
A functioning lifecycle policy can still miss objects with unexpected prefixes or tags.
Serving errors
Track missing-object failures for records the application considers published.
Aggressive cleanup can lower cost while silently breaking valid customer content.
lab: Create file states
Model pending, validated, published, and deleted metadata states.
Interrupt publication
Store bytes but fail before updating metadata, then reconcile the orphan.
Interrupt deletion
Delete metadata or enqueue cleanup in a controlled failure scenario.
Replay cleanup
Confirm repeated cleanup cannot remove a different version or tenant's object.
Exercise retention
Keep a retained version while removing an expired temporary upload.
Audit both systems
Compare expected references, object existence, and lifecycle evidence.
takeaway: Cheap object storage still needs ownership, reconciliation, and a tested deletion contract.

title: Search Is a Read Model
hook: A search result can be fast, relevant, and still wrong for the current user.
premise: Treat a search index as a derived view with explicit freshness and authorization requirements. The source of truth remains independently recoverable.
roadmap: Define searchable meaning
Specify tokenization, fields, filters, ranking goals, and access boundaries.
Build from authoritative data
Use stable document identities and versioned transforms for indexing.
Track freshness
Measure delay from source changes to searchable updates and deletions.
Enforce permissions
Apply authorization before returning results, including snippets and counts where required.
Rebuild safely
Create a new index version and validate it before switching traffic.
Test relevance and failure
Use labeled queries, stale documents, deleted records, and permission changes in evaluation.
decisions: Database search
Use database-native search when workload and relevance needs fit its operational envelope.
Complex ranking and high search volume may compete with transactional workloads.
Dedicated search index
Use a search engine when indexing and relevance requirements justify a separate read model.
You now own ingestion lag, reindexing, deletion propagation, and source/index reconciliation.
Hybrid retrieval
Combine lexical and semantic signals when evaluation demonstrates a useful improvement.
Additional ranking and embedding dependencies increase latency, cost, and debugging complexity.
incident: Find stale or unauthorized hits
Search returns removed content or data outside the user's current permissions.
Check source versions
Compare document identity, version, and deletion state with the authoritative store.
Contain exposure
Disable affected results or enforce authoritative permission checks before returning content.
Inspect ingestion lag
Find dropped updates, failed transforms, or consumers behind their source stream.
Repair the index
Reprocess affected identities or rebuild a validated index version.
Test permission changes
Verify revocation and deletion behavior, not only the happy-path relevance score.
metrics: Indexing delay
Measure source-change-to-searchable latency by update and deletion type.
A healthy query latency says nothing about how current the returned data is.
Retrieval quality
Evaluate relevance using a versioned set of queries and labels.
One aggregate score can hide failures for rare but important query classes.
Permission mismatches
Test whether denied documents, snippets, or counts appear in controlled authorization cases.
Security checks cannot be replaced by an assumption that the index is already filtered correctly.
lab: Create a tiny corpus
Use synthetic documents with versions, tenants, and explicit permissions.
Index deterministic fields
Record the transform and tokenization settings used by the index.
Change and delete records
Measure how updates propagate into results and snippets.
Revoke access
Verify that a previously visible document stops appearing for the affected user.
Build a second index
Reindex from source and compare correctness and relevance before switching.
Evaluate failures
Include missing updates, delayed ingestion, and malformed documents in the test report.
takeaway: Search quality includes relevance, freshness, and permission correctness, not just response time.
